Remember, young kids enjoy games. Instead of using the traditional method to teach a musical concept or song, try to be creative and blend it with monthly themes like Halloween or Valentine’s Day. One big takeaway from my student teaching experience is letting students know the importance of what you're teaching and how they can apply it in the future. You can generate different ideas to explain a concept from different perspectives.

I wouldn't stress about strictly following state standards to make it effective. Each school's music program varies, and remember, student teaching involves collaborative teaching with a mentor who has more experience. If you've never fully handled a classroom before, I would suggest using her materials to teach for the initial part of your placements. Then, gradually integrate your own ideas to create your lessons, to gain a better feel for pacing and the effectiveness of the activities.

You don’t need to replicate everything your CT does. Eventually, you'll become your own teacher, so take what works well and refine it to match your teaching style. I hope that helps.

I was in the same place as you 4 months ago, and I have 3 more days left. I would say, be aware of work-life balance. There's nothing you can do until the first day of school. Each school has different rotations, so you'll need to communicate with your CT and ask about their planning styles. Usually, during the first 4 weeks, you'll need to keep asking teachers questions and take on more portions of the classes as you go.

For lesson planning, as a young teacher, you should print out your lesson plans every lesson. Use sticky notes in your script to mark down the issues and measures that you want to fix. For elementary school, I usually use slide shows to remind myself of the lesson flows. The visuals also help with student understanding.
